utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Thursday, the 4th of December, 2008. I would like, first of all, to greet Mr. Tihic, the representatives of the OTP, as well as their associates. I would like to greet Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us in this courtroom, the Registrar and the usher, without forgetting the interpreters. We shall resume the cross-examination today. Mr. Seselj, you have one hour and 15 minutes left, according to the calculations made by our Registrar. I shall give you the floor for the rest of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Cross-examination by Mr. Seselj [Continued]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, right up until 1990, you were a member of the League of Communists, right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you saw that the party had in fact not been a success, it had fallen through, you didn't see any prospects there, but you waivered with respect to becoming a member in one of these newly-established parties?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, could you let me answer that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not too long.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say just "yes" or "no," so I'd like to explain. I had a dilemma for a long time because I lived in a time and system that were different. My father was a partisan. I'm from a partisan family, and the party of the day was the organiser of the uprising, and there was a tradition linked to the party which existed at the time, so I was facing a dilemma in my family, too, whether I should go and join up with one of the other newly-established parties. And when I saw that the League of Communists could not survive and that, because of all the baggage it had with it and all the various processes that were developing, it would have no clout and no power, I opted for the Party of Democratic Action, first of all, because I thought that that party would devote most of its activities to Bosnia and Herzegovina, not to only one nation, one ethnic group, but Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole, whether it was in a Yugoslavia that would be federal, confederal, or whatever. And in that particular party, they did not have a platform of forming Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state, but to protect the rights and freedoms of the people living within it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at the beginning, you had a great deal of reservations towards the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA party, and its leader, Alija Izetbegovic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any reservations or special dilemmas. Actually, my dilemma was whether I was going to join that party or whether I was going to remain in the League of Communists. But I saw that the League of Communists was incapable of fulfilling and meeting up the times that were coming, so I thought that of all the Bosnian parties, it was the SDA party that would most be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had problems with people in Samac who formed branches of the SDA; you didn't consider that they were worthy of your trust and confidence?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not right. It was just that people -- it was people who didn't understand politics and weren't engaged in politics in those times. They were people that had secondary-level education without any political experience, experience in economic matters and so on. And when I was on the ticket, the other people there were mostly tradesmen, people who had various skills, bakers and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that was later. That was when you already became a member. But you were wavering, because you considered that they weren't people who enjoyed particular respect in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were ordinary people, working people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, the Prosecutor disclosed a document to me, I wouldn't have got it otherwise, a text of yours called "Remembrance." And I use that word "sjecanje" because you use the "ch" in the spelling. It should be "sjecanja." But you wrote it for the State Commission for Collecting Data about War Crimes?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wrote that when I emerged from the camp, because as time went on, I thought that I was beginning to forget things and the order and sequence of events, what happened in what camp, so in order not to forget those events or, rather, mix them up and put events that took place in one camp into another, I wrote this book, "Remembrance," which would help me to remember the sequence of events, how they followed each other chronologically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it helped me to get a better knowledge of your life and experience, because they have severed my contacts with my associates, so it was only on the basis of documents provided me by the Prosecution that I was able to prepare this cross-examination. But, anyway, on page 2 of that very extensive text, 60 pages, you say you attended the founding assemblies of all -- or, rather, the promotional meetings of all the parties that were set up in Bosanski Samac, and then you say that this party, the Party of Democratic Action, didn't suit you. And I'm quoting you now: "It was mostly a group of people who did not enjoy any particular respect in the environment of Samac, and people who had come into Samac from other places. So they were ordinary people, and various activists talked to me and we discussed becoming a member of the SDA. They offered me the post of president, if only I would accept becoming a member of the party," because they thought that if you joined, you would draw in the more respected citizens of Sarajevo, prominent citizens of Sarajevo. So that's your assessment about the SDA when it was formed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly all the parties at the beginning had this kind of problems with the membership, and when power was set up, they found that they had a lack of well-educated people with political experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you thought about joining the Liberal Party, led by Rasim Kadic; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and those were the dilemmas that I spoke about. I had this dilemma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were disillusioned by that party, too, and then you gave up on the idea?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I almost came to the party building to join up, but then they issued a statement, a proclamation, which reminded me of the political work of the League of Communists, because it was Rasim Kadic was only present at the establishment meeting of the SDA. Because he was there, they criticised him for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you thought they weren't tolerant enough?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, because it was quite normal that as a member of one party, you would attend founding meetings of other parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand you completely, because I attended these Democratic Party when it was formed, but it was -- nothing was furthest from my mind than to become a member of that party.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down and speak one at a time. Otherwise, it's impossible to interpret. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj and Mr. Tihic, once again I'm sorry to interrupt you. The interpreters are having such a hard time following you, so please, both of you, slow down, speak slower, and please do observe a short pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say here that at the first elections, only 50 per cent of the Muslims voted for the SDA; right? The rest voted for the other parties?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was on the basis of the results that were achieved. The Bosniak electorate could vote for four MPs, four seats, and the SDA two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the second part of 1991, you began to help the SDA in its work, and sometime in autumn you became a member; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had become a member earlier on, in 1990, but in 1991 I was elected president of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it says here "1991," and then somebody corrected that and put "1990." So you say the autumn of 1990?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was on the ticket, on the party ticket, and the elections were on the 18th of October; that is to say, before the 18th of October, I became a member of the SDA in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was already clear then that the communists would lose the elections, and it was your goal to bring as many respected members of the community into the SDA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't only my objective. Many prominent citizens, Bosniaks, tried to prevail upon me to join the SDA. They said, "You're a lawyer. It's easier for you. We have -- we work for the state, but we'll join up later on."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In September 1990, the founding meeting in Bosanski Samac was held, at which Alija Izetbegovic took part?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, I was surprised to hear one of your answers, your answer, in fact, to my last question before we broke for the day, when you said that you never supported Adil Zulfikarpasic, Muhamed Filipovic, and their Bosniak-Muslim organisation, whereas in your statement on page 3, I see the following, you say that several days before this assembly at which Alija Izetbegovic took part, and then I quote you: "There was a rift in the party when Adil Zulfikarpasic and Tunjo Filipovic separated." Tunjo Filipovic. "Tunjo," that's the nickname for Muhamed Filipovic, "and that created a dilemma for me, whether to join up with the party because at that time I preferred their views, and that was the reason why I did not join the SDA membership publicly on that occasion." So those are your own words. You say here that you preferred their political positions and that you supported them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was one of the dilemmas, why I had to decide whether or not to join the SDA party, because Professor Muhamed Filipovic was a respected figure, personage, Zulfikarpasic, too. We had that on one side, and Alija Izetbegovic was very popular on the other amongst the people. So I gave the matter a lot of thought. And then we had the personage of Fikret Abdic looming, but that did not mean that I supported some of the late activities of Muhamed Filipovic and Zulfikarpasic, such as the agreement you mentioned yesterday, the agreement with Milosevic, the historical agreement as it was referred to, and I said that I did not support that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Adil Zulfikarpasic was a very prominent personage among the Serbian people as well until his death two or three years ago; do you agree, he was well respected?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was well respected among the Bosniaks, among the Serbs and the Croats, because he was a person of great tolerance. He was an emigre who helped Bosnia and Herzegovina and the political prisoners even before, before the times of communism, and among others Mr. Izetbegovic, and then he set up the Bosniak Institute in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he was a very prominent democratic and not burdened by religious fundamentalism?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a great democratic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We agree on that point. Now, you really do say here that as the elections grew near, you had to decide, and in the meantime Fikret Abdic joined the SDA as well. And then there were large rallies that were held in Foca and Velika Kladusa, magnanimous meetings, and you decided to join the party then?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those dilemmas went on throughout 1990 for a few months, seven or eight months, in fact, and certainly those meetings and the fact that prominent Bosniaks had joined up with the SDA tipped the scales, and I joined too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here on page 3, you say that the Muslims of Samac, from a distance, viewed the activities of the SDA. Some supported it and were in favour -- well, mostly quiet support -- and the other section of the population publicly opposed it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims of Samac, like the majority of Bosnians, liked Yugoslavia. They liked that time, those times of Josip Broz Tito. It provided security and safety, both social and in every other respect, and they were not able to accept changes as quickly. And if I had the dilemma, and if I can say so, I understood things better than the ordinary man in the street and it was a dilemma for me, then they had an even bigger one. So the Muslims of Samac liked Yugoslavia, and the Bosniaks generally in Bosnia-Herzegovina liked Yugoslavia, and even in Bosnia and Herzegovina you still have streets named after Marshal Tito and remembrances of Avnoj, the anti-fascist, liberation of Yugoslavia and so on, and many Muslims joined up the 4th --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Many Muslims joined the 4th Detachment under the 17th Tactical group; isn't that right? We talked about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some Bosniaks did join up, those who still thought that the JNA was an army belonging to us all. They believed in Yugoslavia and that it could be preserved, and those who had been linked to the security structures previously and the army especially so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there's another factor. The Muslims of Samac were never prone, in the majority, to any religious fundamentalism. They were not prone to place religion up above everything else in the life of the society. Of course, that doesn't mean they weren't good Muslims. They were good Muslims, some more, some less, but they always took into account religious tolerance, right, and couldn't be compared to certain environments in Bosnia, where the situation was quite different?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, our historical experience, when it comes to life in Bosanski Samac and that general area, we lived with the Serbs and the Croats, and our life together was positive. We always kept our traditions and our religion, but there were no expulsions, no persecution. That's how I behaved, and that's how all the other Muslims of Samac behaved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A large number of these Muslims did not like the policies of Alija Izetbegovic. Alija Izetbegovic was already well known as an Islamic fundamentalist and a pan-Islamist; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you saw the outcome of the election. After all, at that time, when people were still not fully aware of what was going on, 50 per cent supported the SDA, the list that I talked about, the ticket that I talked about. It really did not include the best people. That is to say that the SDA and Alija Izetbegovic won half of the votes in towns. However, it's the SDP that prevailed in that election throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. It wasn't Alija Izetbegovic. Whereas in Samac, the Bosniak Muslims, that was the case only in town. The SDA or the HDZ and the SDS did not win a majority in any one of the towns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us not evade the essence of my question. Do you agree with me that a large number of citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslims included, believed that Alija Izetbegovic represented the hard-line Islamic option, that he was a fundamentalist and pan-Islamist?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree that it was a large number. It was a small number of the citizens, and that is shown by the outcome of the election, because the SDA did win about three-quarters of the Bosniak Muslim vote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that was significantly contributed to by the fact that the three nationalist parties got together and people thought that this would strike the right kind of balance. If these parties stayed together, then their negative aspects would be neutralised and they would have to seek compromise and lead Bosnia and Herzegovina with a proper understanding?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now, why people voted the way they voted, we can discuss that for quite a while, can't we? And in the late President Izetbegovic, they saw a victim of political persecution, and people tend to express solidarity with people like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No doubt he was a victim of the communist regime, and he was held responsible for the text that he hadn't even published before that.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was held responsible on account of what was called "verbal offences." What he wrote was always taken out of the context of what he was trying to say, and he was sentenced to harsh sentences that he did not deserve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know whether you know, but the first petition that was organised in favour of Izetbegovic and his group came from my hands. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I know about the Belgrade intellectuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the Belgrade intellectuals, there was this meeting in Komiza on the island of Vis, in the birthplace of Anto Fiamenko, a well-known sociologists, and it was a gathering of sociologists, and I initiated this petition that was signed by sociologists from Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina. That doesn't matter. We do agree that he was convicted and spent time in prison for no reason whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've been saying yourself, sir, he was not a fundamentalist, he was not an extremist. You wouldn't have signed a petition for a man who was a fundamentalist and an extremist. He was a free thinker. At that time, you weren't allowed to write what it was that you thought, and that is why he was held responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that everyone can think whatever they want and they can publish their thoughts. However, if the thoughts are bad, then they should be subjected to public criticism. People shouldn't be sent to prison because of that. That was my position in view of Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, but he was not an extremist or a fundamentalist. You know, in the war, where Izetbegovic was in power, there were no mass crimes. He prevented that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Already in 1980, this notorious Islamic declaration of his was published. This was in 1989, in actual fact. And after that, it was published several times. After that, there were other editions, too. I'm just going to show you, by citing a few examples, that he was a pan -Islamist and a Muslim fundamentalist. I have here before me the first volume of the selected works of Alija Izetbegovic that was published in 2005. However, up until then, this book had been published several times. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was published before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I can remember correctly, the first time was in 1989.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're right on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slobodan Masic, who was an independent publisher, published it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. He says in his book that his objective was to create a synthesis of ideas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Gentlemen, the interpreters are complaining. Since you are both intellectuals, we are able to follow the question and the answers, because we understand the question very quickly and we know which way the answers will go. But the interpreters' job is somewhat different, and every time they lose track, and you can see this on the screen, that they're having a hard time. So once again, Witness, you are also a culprit. Please wait before you answer. You may feel that we understand your language, but we don't understand your language. We understand which way the questions and the answers are going, but we follow, but the interpreters can't keep up, and the court interpreter -- the court reporter will have to leave blanks on the transcript. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Already in the preface of this Islamic declaration of his, he speaks of his objective; to create a synthesis of ideas that are otherwise heard in different parts of the Islamic world and, as he says, and now I'm quoting --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "To move on from ideas and plans to organised action in order to have this implemented. The struggle for new objectives does not start today." This is on page 130: "On the contrary, the history of this struggle already knows its sahids and the pages that were written about suffering and victims. After all, this is the result of the sacrifice made by individuals and groups. The magnitude of the tasks and the difficulties calls for organised action on the part of millions." Tell me, please, he speaks of sahids here. These are martyrs of Jihad, of the holy war for the faith; those are sahids, right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise for the speed at which we've been speaking. I think that it's Mr. Seselj who's been setting the pace, and then I tend to hurry a bit too much as well. Mr. Izetbegovic did not, in a single one of his texts, call for violence. A sahid is a person who lost his or her life on God's path, as it is said. It can be in war and in peacetime for certain objectives, or the faith, Islam, et cetera. However, not in a single book, including this one, "The Islamic Declaration," is there any reference made by Izetbegovic about some movement that would mean violence. He believed that the Muslims had to be changed, that they had to adjust to the changed situation in the world, that in a way time has left them behind, that they were not following contemporary processes either in scholarly or societal matters. That is what he spoke about at many Islamic conferences, when he addressed criticism to the Muslims of the world because they were not adjusting. He was a man of coexistence, tolerance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, please, let us speak in more specific terms with regard to particular matters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could all other microphones please be switched off. There is a great deal of background noise and we can't hear the speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know that in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the Muslim-Croat federation, calls all the Muslims who lost their lives during the war sahids and their cemeteries are called Sahidsko Mezarija?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come you can say "no"?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll explain now. In our federation, references are made to the sahids and to the soldiers who got killed. Both terms are used. So sahids and killed soldiers are persons who lost their lives during the war. They were buried together. They were buried at cemeteries, "mezarluks," and people called them "sahidluks" [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, you were quite clear now. In the law it says, sahids and killed soldiers. Sahids refers to killed Muslims, and killed soldiers refers to killed soldiers. Perhaps some Serbs got killed in your army as well, and who knows. Who knows what other ethnic backgrounds were there. Perhaps a Jew got killed, or who knows who else. However, the word "sahids" refers to all Muslims who got killed. You see, they lost their lives for the faith. They're holy warriors.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If it's not true, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true, because sahids who lost their lives and soldiers who lost their lives, this pertains to Muslims, who can be sahids as well. There are Bosniaks who are atheists as well. There are "sahidluks" where Serbs are buried, too. At Kovaci, for instance, there are Serbs who also got killed, who fought in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the very outset. There were about 20 per cent of the members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who had other ethnic backgrounds, and it is only natural for such persons we cannot use the term "sahidi." I think that not even the Bosniaks are sahids.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, Mr. Tihic, all right, they're not, but there are very many of those who are sahids, which is proof that they took part in a religious war and that they are martyrs are fell for the faith. From that point of view, they are paid tribute to, and I'm not opposed to that, but let us establish the facts. And their kinsmen respect them for that and the official authorities respect them for that. They are martyrs who fell for the faith, which means that they took part in a religious war. A religious war, in Islamic tradition, is called "Jihad," and this Jihad is what Izetbegovic mentions in his "Islamic Declaration"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it's not, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to answer why it is not the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They got killed while defending Bosnia-Herzegovina. They defended their country, they defended their people, they defended their family, they defended their own lives. It is not only on account of faith, as you've been saying. See, many people who got killed were not even practicing Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is Alija Izetbegovic who is refuting what you say. On page 131 of the "Islamic Declaration," I quote --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "People and individuals who espoused Islam are incapable after that of living and dying for any other ideal. It is inconceivable that a Muslim would make a sacrifice for an emperor or a ruler, no matter what his name may be, or for the glory of a nation, party, or anything of the kind, because according to the strongest possible Islamic instincts, in this he recognises a kind of paganism and idolatry. A Muslim can lose his life only with the name of Allah on his lips and for the glory of Islam, or he can flee from the battlefield." That is what is stated in Alija Izetbegovic's book. Have you read that book of his?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read the book. However, you are taking -- you are just taking some excerpts out of context apart from the substance of that book and the message conveyed by the book. You can do that with any book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I haven't finished yet. In every book, you can find some sections that have a different meaning when taken out of context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, precisely on this day in 1644, I believe it was, Cardinal Richelieu died, and he said a well-known thing, "Give me just one word, one line, from any piece or body of writing, and I will find cause for him to be sent to the gallows." I agree that this is a dangerous thing. However, this involves a large number of quotations, and the book itself is called "The Islamic Declaration." I cannot read the entire book for you. Now, the OTP has the entire book translated into English, and they can submit this to the Trial Chamber, if they haven't already, so who wishes to read the book, can read the book. However, since the OTP has also been showing just brief excerpts of your interview to TV Novi Sad yesterday, we did not view it in its entirety, it's impossible to present everything in its entirety here, I'm compelled only to deal with a few quotations. For example, yet another quotation from part of the Declaration where Izetbegovic advocates an Islamic order, and he says: "The briefest definition of 'Islamic order 'defines it as the unity of faith and law, upbringing and force, and the spiritual community of the state, and voluntariness and coercion." These are his words, and everyone in Bosnia knew that; Bosniaks, Muslims, Croats, Serbs, et cetera. And then he moves on to say: "As the synthesis of these components, the Islamic Order has two basic postulates: the Islamic society and the Islamic authority. The first is substance and the second is form of the Islamic Order. The Islamic society without an Islamic authority is an unfinished one, it is impotent. Islamic authority without an Islamic society is either utopia or violence." And most importantly Izetbegovic says here: "A Muslim, for the most part, does not exist as an individual. If he wishes to live and to live on as a Muslim, he has to create a setting, a community, an order for him. He has to change the world or he will be changed himself. History does not know of a single Islamic movement which was not at the same time a political movement. It is due to the fact that Islam is a faith, but at the same time it is a philosophy, a morality, an order of things, a style, an atmosphere; in a word, an integral way of life. One cannot believe in an Islamic way and live and govern in a non-Islamic way or have fun in a non-Islamic way." You see that this is an Islamic fundamentalist writing this, according to his very own ideology; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you allow me to respond now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've been letting you respond all along. I've just been asking you questions, and you're providing the answers.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you put a question that is perhaps a page long. It contains different statements that I do not agree with, you see, and lest there be a wrong impression involved, you're referring to, say, page 131. The book has 150 pages. You quoted here two or three pages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, they take one sentence out of a speech of mine and they ask me to spend my life in prison. They asked that I be sentenced for life, you see.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just finish, and may I just make a comment? May I just make a comment in terms of what you have been stating? You know, the personality and the works of the late Izetbegovic cannot be viewed only in the quotations from a certain book. His entire life is the life of a humanist, of a tolerant man, who suffered and was held accountable because of his thoughts. There is no extremism or fundamentalism in the case of Izetbegovic. There is no intention of forcing others to behave the way he wants them to. He was always in favour of a Bosnia-Herzegovina where the Serbs and the Croats and the Jews and everybody else would be equal and where they would respect one another. That is in the spirit of Islam as a faith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I have no intention of insulting either you or Alija Izetbegovic. We were opponents in war, and I'm now asking you questions based on quotations. It's up to you to answer, and I have no reason to believe you have any reason to be angry with me. On page 145, Alija Izetbegovic draws this conclusion. I quote: "Certainly, one must make the conclusion about the incompatibility of Islam and Islamic systems. There can be no peace or coexistence between Islamic faith and non-Islamic societal institutions. Assuming the right to order the world its own way, Islam clearly excludes the possibility of action of any foreign ideology in its own area. If you think this is a call to tolerance, that's your right." On the next page, he says: "There is no secular principle. The state is supposed to uphold the moral concepts of religion." This is a well-known view of Alija Izetbegovic, isn't it, because his book has been published in many editions and had a wide audience. Every semi-literate man in Bosnia-Herzegovina, be it Serb, Croat or Muslim, has read it.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer? President Izetbegovic has written books, and as you said, there is a collection of his books that he wrote in different periods of his life. "The Islamic Declaration" belongs to an earlier period. And President Izetbegovic, like any man, changed over his lifetime, changed his thinking, his views, which is perfectly logical, just like you did, just like I did, just like all of us do. I could give you excerpts from other later books and quote many things that reflect the real personality of Izetbegovic as a humanist who advocated peaceful coexistence and tolerance. When he withdrew from politics, he got congratulations from the president of the US, from France, from many other states, not because they feared him but because they respected him as a man who represented peace, negotiation, agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what regard I have for Jacques Chirac or Bill Clinton? They are all disgusting to me. But that doesn't matter. We have the right to be different. "The Islamic Declaration" is the major work of Alija Izetbegovic, that is his main work, the work of his life. That is indubitable. This is what he says about the upbringing of the people: "The upbringing of the people, especially the means of mass influence, radio, television, radio and film, should be in the hands of the people whose Islamic moral and intellectual integrity is beyond reproach. It must not be allowed that these media fall into the hands of immoral people who would transfer their own deviations to others. What would we do if the TV tower sends to the people completely contradictory messages?" In keeping with these views that he held, the State Television in Sarajevo and other major and minor media began to act; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on. On page 154, he says: "Were it not for the --" Sorry: "There can be no Islamic order without independence and freedom and vice versa. There is no independence and freedom without Islam. This last position is important. The Islamic order can be permanent only if it is a sign of freedom conquered, if a people has found itself, then found its internal force without which it cannot fill this freedom with content and preserve its independence." And then he is goes on to say: "The real support that the Islamic people gives to the regime in power is in direct proportion with the Islamic character of that power. It is therefore the lesser, the farther the regime is from Islam. Non-Islamic regimes, therefore, remain completely without this support, and thus willy-nilly have to seek support from foreigners." And now, when Alija Izetbegovic pushes this ideology at any cost, even at the cost of war, and seeks independence for Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, first and foremost, for everything to be clear, let me tell you that we are not here to try Mr. Izetbegovic. Secondly, regarding relevance, you have read this declaration. Fine. It would be good to know when it was written, whether it was written before Mr. Izetbegovic was head of state or while he was heading the state, because it would be very different. Now, regarding relevance, what are you trying to demonstrate with this book?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to demonstrate the nature of authority and government that Alija Izetbegovic tried to inaugurate in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I'm demonstrating that the Serbs, not even at the cost of their lives, wanted to reconcile themselves with that government. For speculative reasons, the Croats supported him at first, but then went to war with him in 1993. And finally, even today's efforts of politicians in Bosnia to annul Republika Srpska, to turn Bosnia and Herzegovina into a unitarian state, follow this thrust of Islamic and pan-Islamic domination, and you chaired the trial here, Mr. President, of people indicted for engaging Islamic Mujahedin in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you had the occasion to familiarise yourself with the crimes of these Mujahedin. You have evidence of the involvement of al-Qaeda in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there is al-Qaeda network in Bosnia-Herzegovina still today. You heard about Abu Hamza and many others. You heard a witness testify about an intelligence centre in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I must say that personally, I still do not understand what is the relevance to your Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to demonstrate that for the Serbian people, there was only one option; to stay within Yugoslavia or to create their own state in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Serbian people could never, by any means, reconcile themselves to the regime led by a man whose major work I just represented to you through a few brief quotations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Mussemeyer. The witness would like to answer, because I believe that he is being called upon. But you wanted to say something, Mr. Mussemeyer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I don't want to prevent the witness to answer. I have only a short observation. Mr. Seselj is, like usual, quoting from documents which he did not provide to the Prosecution before. This is unprofessional. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I have to respond to what the Prosecutor just said. I said to the court officer to convey to the Prosecution that I would be using the statement of Mr. Tihic made available to me by the OTP and the book of Alija Izetbegovic, "The Islamic Declaration." I said that -- I conveyed that verbally to the court officer, and I thought it was arranged. Now, where would I photocopy this document to give it again to the Prosecution, and where would I photocopy the book that the Prosecution certainly has? You do have that book, and you must have read it. And when you examined Sefer Halilovic at length, that book was also used. There are a thousand pages of that examination of Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, I believe that the OTP must have Mr. Izetbegovic's book. If you don't, I mean, that would be quite incredible. Maybe you don't have it yourself, but I believe that the OTP has it. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I agree with this, and I'm not sure that we have it, but I think we have it. But it would be professional to provide the Prosecution, before the cross-examination starts, that the accused has the intention to quote from this book, that we can prepare ourselves. And for the -- it is true that we got information from the Registrar just before we started this morning that Mr. Seselj is willing to quote from Mr. Tihic's [sic] memories just to assist the Trial Chamber. These memories are part of the Prosecution exhibit list. They are number 65 ter 2094, and I think it should be moved into evidence, because the accused is quoting from this, and therefore it has to go into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, you wanted to answer. Please, you have the floor. You've listened to what Mr. Seselj said regarding the relevance of his line of questioning. I'm not going to sum up what he said. You know exactly what he said just as well as I do. But what did you want to say? You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I wanted to respond to your question addressed to Mr. Seselj when that book was written. The book, "The Islamic Declaration," was written approximately 20 years before Alija Izetbegovic was elected president. That is the first thing I wished to say. Now, what kind of a book was it? Because of that book, he was, among other things, indicted, and you heard from Mr. Seselj a moment ago that he had voiced his support to Alija Izetbegovic himself during that trial and protested against that trial. That book was the subject of a trial in which Mr. Seselj was, in a way, involved. These stories about al-Qaeda, these are fabrications against Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is a country in which Bosniak Muslims, as an autonomous people, have lived for hundreds of years together with Serbs and Croats, and they adjust their behaviour to the environment in which they live. There is no extremism or fundamentalism there, especially not al-Qaeda. Not a single terrorist act, not a single attack has been registered in all this time against any building, against any individual, against any representative of the International Community where the Muslims live. All these stories are part of a propaganda that is an attempt to justify crimes and everything that happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, the only question that sums everything up is the question I will ask myself. You have responsibilities with the SDA, so as far as you're concerned, could you tell us whether, at the time of Mr. Izetbegovic, the SDA was a religious political party or a secular political party, among which members that were of a certain religion could exist? In a nutshell, that's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Party of Democratic Action was a secular party, not because I say so but because that is written in its programme, its platform, its declaration, and it's in the document of registration of that party. And it was also secular in its action, in its work for Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state of equal peoples. It was said clearly at its founding Assembly that Bosnia and Herzegovina can be neither Serbian, nor Croat, nor Muslim. It belongs to all those three and other peoples who feel the same way. It is true, at the time of its founding, it was also struggling for ethnic and religious rights of the Muslims. It was one of our objectives, because the Muslims were not recognised under their name, "Bosniaks," and some other rights that other people in Yugoslavia enjoyed were not granted to Muslims yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, you have said that Alija Izetbegovic never advocated violence in "The Islamic Declaration." I can refute that immediately. On page 162, he says, I quote: "Emphasising the priority of religious moral renewal cannot mean nor can be interpreted to mean that the Islamic order is achievable without Islamic government. This position only means that our path does not start with conquering power, but with conquering people, and that Islamic renewal is, first of all, an upheaval in the area of upbringing and only then politics. We have to preach politics first. We have to be politicians and then soldiers. Our weapons are books and words. When will these means be joined by power? The choice of this moment is always a specific question. It depends on a number of factors. Still, one general rule can be observed: The Islamic movement should and can proceed to take over power as soon as it is numerically strong enough not only to topple the current power, but to build a new Islamic power. This is very important, because destruction and construction do not require the same degree of psychological and material preparation. Going too early in this is as dangerous as going too late." Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are certainly not right, and you are never right with regard to Mr. Izetbegovic. Mr. Alija Izetbegovic speaks of spiritual renewal here, because in the past 50 years the Bosniak Muslims, like other peoples, had been under an atheist government, and he's speaking primarily of a kind of spiritual renewal, revival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You deny that Alija Izetbegovic was a pan-Islamist, ideologically, and here I have proof on 164 that he was a pan-Islamist. He says: "In one of the thesis for the Islamic order of today, we stated that an actual function of the Islamic order is the aspiration to gather all Muslims and all Islamic communities in the world. In today's circumstances, this aspiration means a struggle to create a greater Islamic federation from Morocco to Indonesia, from tropical Africa to Central Asia." And then on the next page, 165, he goes on to say: "How does it happen that this popular pan-Islamism, indubitably present in the form of the feelings of the masses, remains without any influence on the actual policies of Islamic states? Why does it remain at the level of feelings? Why doesn't it rise to the level of awareness of a common Islamic fate?" And then he goes on to explain. Is it proof of his pan-Islamist orientation?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is no proof of anything of the kind. He just states his view on the condition of Islam throughout the world, including various countries with various dictatorships that exist in the world. That's probably what he meant to say, but it's very difficult for me to comment here and now, "The Islamic Declaration" of President Izetbegovic, in the context of your quotations and excerpts taken out of the whole, the entirety of his life's actions and work. It was very different from what he was 20 years later, when many circumstances changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, you are the successor of Alija Izetbegovic, at the head of the SDA party. You are the legate of his ideology. Even in the middle of the night, if awakened suddenly, I can always answer questions about great Serb nationalists, whose successor I am, from Laza Kostic and other great figures and what they stated in their major works, and in the same way I expect you to know well the ideology of your predecessor and your spiritual father, if I may put it so. This is his -- the major work of his life. He answers this question in this way, and I quote: "The answer to this question lies in the fact that contrary to the feelings of popular masses, there is the action of educated people, educated in the West, and they were pan-Islamists. The actions were contrary to feelings, and in this sense any action will remain impossible. Contemporary pan-Islamism is, in fact, an aspiration to harmonise feelings with action. The state determines the character and the fate of Islamism in today's world." And then he comes down heavily upon various Arab regimes of secular character; the Syrian, Iraqi, Tunisian, et cetera. Everything of secular nature is a target of his attacks. He is seeking a fundamentalist regime; isn't that correct, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't, that's not so. Mr. Izetbegovic spoke about the lack of unity among the Muslims in the world. He spoke about that very frequently and said that the Muslims were not -- did not profess solidarity, the rich Muslims with the poor Muslims, and it was especially President Izetbegovic who was opposed to dictatorship. And what you mentioned, Syria and Tunisia and those other countries you mentioned, they were dictatorships, they were Soviets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I visited some of those countries, for instance, Syria, I was in Iraq, and those were countries which were of a very progressive character, highly secular and religiously tolerant; whereas the countries that are an example, as far as Alija Izetbegovic is concerned, like Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and similar countries, cannot be taken to be examples, good examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, to try and streamline these questions, it seems -- we stand to be corrected. However, it seems that Mr. Seselj is putting forward the idea that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and amongst others, those in the Republika Srpska, got together and joined forces because they feared an Islamic state as part of a pan-Islamic order. This is the underlying theory behind Mr. Seselj's questions. You are a major player in all of this. What do you think about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not correct. Mr. Seselj is attaching too great an importance to the book, "The Islamic Declaration." In the life and work of Izetbegovic, Izetbegovic himself, it doesn't have that importance. And Mr. Seselj said that he was opposed to the -- to taking Izetbegovic to trial. The Serbs, in 1990, when they voted -- or, rather, the Serbian party called upon the Serbs to vote for Izetbegovic on the Izetbegovic ticket, and to vote for him personally. Why would they do that? Why would they call upon the Serbs to vote for Izetbegovic if Izetbegovic was some sort of fundamentalist who wanted to see a Muslim Bosnia? So that's just not true. In his life and work, from his birth to the death, none of that existed, and what Mr. Seselj is saying now is politicising and justifying something. The conflict came about because the Serbs wanted to remain in Yugoslavia. It's quite simple. Yugoslavia suited them. It suited the Bosniaks, too, for that matter, but not because of Alija Izetbegovic's book and not out of a fear that he could impose some sort of society which would -- especially not an Islamic society. We all know that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that could never be the case. It could not be the case and should not be the case anywhere, let alone in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where there are at least three ethnicities that have lived together for centuries. Nobody could accept that; none of the Muslims. The Bosniaks could not accept a society of that kind, because we've been living in a different environment for hundreds of years. We have Orthodox, we have Catholics, we have Jews. So there is no grounds and support for that kind of an idea, nor did the idea ever exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I believe you've heard of a prominent intellectual who stood up in defending the freedom of thought of a certain man who thanked him for that, and he addressed him in the following words. He said, "Sir, you are saying stupid things throughout, but I will fight to my last breath for your right to say those things, those stupid things." Now, I did not think that Alija Izetbegovic's "Islamic Declaration" was not a serious text. I always thought that it was. But I was an adversary of ideas contained in that Declaration. Nevertheless, I considered that Alija Izetbegovic had the right to present his views, and that is why I defended him, as I would defend anybody else who is taken to task for his beliefs. Now, when his beliefs and his thinking is inaugurated through a political movement, and when it becomes a concrete and specific political goal, then you must understand that there are people who did not agree to live with things like that. Yugoslavia was a safe house both for the Serbs and Muslims, even the rump Yugoslavia; isn't that right, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right, it is not the way you say it. Nowhere in Izetbegovic's political activities were goals opposed that were contained in the "Islamic Declaration," either in the Party of Democratic Action or anywhere else, and President Izetbegovic, on the one hand, held the -- he had his books on one side and his political programme on the other. What he wrote and what he thought about, especially when those thoughts are extracted and put out of context, they can take on a different meaning than the meaning intended by Izetbegovic, although what Mr. Seselj quoted, all those things can be interpreted in quite the opposite manner, quite different to what Mr. Seselj is doing. And when it came to the survival of Yugoslavia, we Bosniaks -- well, it was in our interests for Yugoslavia to be preserved and to live on, but the Serbs and the Croats formed Yugoslavia and so they were the only ones who could safeguard and preserve it. The Bosniaks could not do that. And we did everything in our power to preserve Yugoslavia and Izetbegovic, together with Gligorov, put forward the proposal for a staggered federation and confederation, and we knew that we would be the ones to suffer most in the war, and we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic -- Mr. Tihic. I misspoke and said "Izetbegovic." That was a slip of the tongue. Mr. Tihic, your party, already in 1991, started preparations for the war. You set up the Patriotic League, the Green Berets, and you as the president of the municipal branch of the party in Bosanski Samac, also took certain steps, and you testify about that in this statement of yours. On page 7, for example, you say that you organised professional seminars, you from the municipal boards, that you sent people to be trained in sabotage, and that's to be found on page 7 of your statement. And among those people from Sarajevo who came to train you, there was Sefer Halilovic. You say that, too. He was among them, and you say that on page 7. Then you complain and go on to say that there was great pressure for you to start arming yourselves, and you mentioned names of people, Muslims who insisted upon that most, like Hakija Banacic [phoen], Mitar [indiscernible], Kemal Bobic, and so on, and you say they did nothing specific, but asked that somebody else to that. "We didn't have the money and funds to arm ourselves and all the activities to raise funds fell through because the people of Samac did not want to give money, make donations, and so on two occasions we managed to collect about 3.000 German marks, which was not enough, and at the same time we set up the Crisis Staff in the party, and the Command, and compiled all the documents, such as a war plan," et cetera, and similar things. So you had a war plan, too, didn't you, Mr. Tihic? That's what you say, you say you had one .

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what Mr. Seselj read out is something that I put into my statement and testimony already, because I said that the JNA handed out weapons to the Serbs and that the Croats were busy arming themselves, and that these arms were coming in from Croatia and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It might be a matter of translation, but it is said in the version I have, in the English version, it is not a war plan, it said "a military plan." That for me makes a difference, but it might be by reason of translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "ratne" plan, war plan. The interpreters can check that out for you, "ratne."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic will confirm this straight away. In your statement, you mentioned a war plan or a military plan? This could be two different things, and one might be the same as the other, but it might not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what it says. In actual fact, it was a plan of defence, a protection, protection for the people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Bosniaks in Samac made up 7 per cent of the population, you see, so they could not defend themselves. There were 42 per cent Serbs and 44 per cent Croats, and the Serbs were armed to the teeth, as they say, by the JNA. The Croats were armed in their own way. So all we could do was draw up documents and make plans to try and protect ourselves. Whether it was called a defence plan or a war plan, I really don't know, but the substance is the essential point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, it was mostly the Muslims who were prevalent in town, not in the municipality. There was not a single Muslim village, but in town the Muslims were in the majority. May Mr. Tihic be shown his statement, and on page 7 it says "ratne plan." I'm sure he can't remember. I believe him, but when he sees that, then he will see that it was indeed that he did say "ratne plan," "war plan," if you don't believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't matter what it was called, whether a war plan, a military plan, or a defence plan. The important thing is what we wanted with that plan. And by devising that plan, we made a list of activities about how best to defend ourselves if there was a war conflict, but we had no offensive actions contained in that plan. We didn't say we would attack anybody, or occupy anybody, or take control of anything, or destroy anything. We were just faced with a situation and an environment in which we had to do something. And the plan that we devised could not help us, because we weren't armed, there were much fewer of us, and we weren't armed as much as others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you need 200 kilograms of dynamite? You could have blown up the whole of Samac with that. It says here that you procured 200 kilos of dynamite. Why did you need that then, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my statement that some people from Croatia had brought in that dynamite, and the dynamite remained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because the army stepped in on time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't used, nor did anybody have the intention of using it. They brought it in from somewhere in Croatia, and it was stored there, it was there, and when the army came, it took it away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were a step ahead of you; is that right? Now, you say here you appointed Alija Fitozovic as commander, and then you go on to say that because he was prone towards alcohol, he didn't rank highly in his environment, but his image didn't rank too low, either. He was said to be sympathetic with the Croats, which wasn't bad at the time, but at any case "in view of my influence in the party and among the people, I could replace him at any time and revoke his decision, and that is why I was not afraid of his extremism." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we compiled the plan for preparations, the plan to prepare our defence and protect the population with it, at that time I talked to some Bosniaks who had officer ranks, ranks of reserve officers, and I asked them whether they would accept to help out. They weren't keen to do so. They weren't keen to be included in any of this. There was fear, generally, for security reasons and so on and so forth. But Fitozovic did accept, and he was one of the reserve officers. And Albania Fitozovic didn't do anything bad. Let me make that clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't say he did. Anyway, on page 9, you go on to say the following: "In keeping with an invitation from Alija Izetbegovic, the Muslims," and you're speaking about the Muslims of Samac, "except for a number of local traitors, did not respond to doing any military service or any service in the reserve force." Right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a call-up, an invitation for that. If you'll allow me to finish my answer. President Izetbegovic did tell us not to respond to the call-up and do any military service in the Yugoslav People's Army, because the army was already at war in Slovenia and Croatia. And so the Muslims of Samac mostly respected that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those who responded to the call-up, you called traitors; you say that yourself?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what people called them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj has moved on to another topic. I would like to get back to Fitozovic, who in your statement is mentioned as a captain in the JNA. You mentioned that he was a reserve captain, and it is easy to understand why you had appointed him, because he was an officer. That's the first point. The second point, as far as I can see in your statement, is that under Fitozovic's bed was discovered -- explosives were discovered that had been hidden under the bed, but we can also see, and this you added, that he had gone to fetch them from the Croats. Was there an agreement between the Muslims and the Croats, an understanding between the two, some providing the arms and the explosives to the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had there not been any agreement -- well, I did not take part in the drawing up of any agreement. There are individual cases, and one of those cases, one of those examples, was that Fitozovic went to Slavonski Brod, for instance, and received that from the Croats. But the explosive was never used. It was just found there in his home. I don't know where he kept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but he gets the explosives from the Croats. In other words, does he buy them, does he pay for them on the black market? He buys these explosives from Croats who sell them to him or does he go to see them between, inverted commas, "a cooperation agreement"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he received it free of charge. It was there in Slavonski Brod without any agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this something that is commonly done in the Balkans, to give people weapons free of charge? Well, what was the Croat interest in providing that? For the war in Bosnia to flare up, that was in the Croat interest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably it was an attempt to help the Bosniaks in arming themselves in their defence, that kind of thing, because at that time there was -- the JNA posed the danger. It was the JNA who were a danger to both the Bosniaks and the Croats, and that's why they supplied that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 11, you say that your opinion was that the Croats were always greater friends to you than the Serbs, which was shown through history and subsequent events; right? Now, please do explain to me, when were the Croats better friends to you Muslims, without going into this latest war?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I meant the crimes that, through history, the Serbs committed against the Muslims in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, in Eastern Bosnia, you know what the Chetniks of Draza Mihajlovic did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know of only one case of a mass crime against the Muslims in Foca, and I'm not aware of any other one, and you are not, either.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am. Do you want me to tell you about the crimes in Gorazde in 1942 [Realtime transcript read in error "1992"], you know, when they brought Muslims to the bridge and when they slaughtered several thousand Muslims? And, you know, the partisan detachment from Montenegro prevented that. They did not allow the Muslims to be slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was only one crime against the Muslims in Foca committed by the Chetnik vojvoda Pavle Djurisic from Montenegro. In the Second World War, most of the Muslims were among the Croatian Ustashas and the Domobrans. A lot of Croats were in Hitler's SS Handzar division. There were some Muslims in the so-called village militias, but they were just guarding their villages. There were Muslims in the partisans, a considerable number, and also there were about 10.000 Muslims who were Chetniks. So in the Second World War, Muslims, after all, were not all in favour of one single option. They divided into different options. However, when we go back to your statement --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just respond to what you said just now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to correct something on the record. I think you mentioned, Mr. Tihic, the crimes committed in 1942, and the record says "1992." I think you wanted to respond, Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, there were many crimes that were committed by the Chetniks against Muslims in Eastern Bosnia and elsewhere in Bosnia. Perhaps this is not the right time for me to go into all of that, but Muslims, intellectuals and others, signed an important petition in the Second World War in 1941, in which they condemned the Ustasha movement, and they asked that the Serbs be protected from the crimes that were being committed against them in the Second World War by the Ustasha authorities at the time. So it's not the way Mr. Seselj is putting it, that Muslims were only in favour of the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there Chetniks who were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the Muslims joined the partisans. Some did join the Chetniks, some did join the Ustashas, but most of them were in the ranks of the partisans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's be more specific here. On page 12 of your statement, you said you went to negotiate with Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic. He was commander of the 17th Tactical Group, right, and you ask that the JNA be removed from the location of Uzarija, and you say: "We mentioned as our reason the reaction of the Croatian side, namely, that they could shut off the bridge, and for Bosnia that is the only access or road to Europe. Actually, the real reason was the fact that we knew that arms for Bosnia were being transported across the bridge, so if there were to be a check-point next to Uzarija, imports of arms would be prevented." You say that yourself. You were bothered by the JNA unit near Uzarija because it hindered the import of arms from Croatia into Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, in Bosnia and Herzegovina the JNA quite legally armed the Serbs. All the Serbs were being armed, and they used all their capacities to serve the purposes of the idea of a Greater Serbia. The Muslims were trying to protect themselves so that they would not all get killed, and this weaponry arrived through -- from Croatia through Bosanski Samac, too. I'm not concealing that. I was not involved in that, but it was a thing that people knew, that this happened across this bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You Muslims would have been armed, too, if you had responded to mobilisation call-ups; right? Serbs received call-up papers, and then they had weapons distributed to them. Had you responded to the call-up, you would have also been issued with personal weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. Just a minute, please, let's wait for the interpretation. No, they got weapons even without mobilisation call-ups on the basis of ethnic grounds only.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please, how much time do I have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, it's time for our break. It's already 10.00. We've been sitting for an hour and a half already. We'll have now a 20-minute break. Let me tell you that according to the Registrar, you have ten minutes left, Mr. Seselj, so please try to focus on -- please try to focus your questions, because you only have ten minutes left. We meet again in ten minutes [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. If I remember correctly, the Prosecutor spent a bit more time than was envisaged, a bit more than two hours. I would need an additional ten minutes, in addition to these ten minutes, if possible, and if you also establish that the Prosecutor also overstepped his time limit. I have some other important questions to put to Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You'll have 20 minutes after our 20-minute break. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction earlier, it was a 20-minute break, not ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session after this break, and I give the floor to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this statement of yours, you say how you were conducting these campaigns to collect funds from 200 private entrepreneurs from Samac to pay for the SDA and the reserve police during the guards and also to have bread for dinners and so on. Your detachment already started patrolling Samac, didn't it, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement of mine shows that we had collected a total of 3.000 marks, which was insufficient. Arms could not be bought from that money. We used that here for fuel, per diems, bread for the reserve policemen. We also provided some compensation, because Serbs and Croats, as reserve policemen, did not respond to call-ups from the reserve public security station, and very often there was no security on the bridge across the Sava River. So for the most part, this was done by reservists of Bosniak ethnicity. We only had guards at the entry points into Samac. There was no patrols. These check-points were there at night in the fear that someone would enter Samac during the night and commit crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in your statement, you say the second group consisted of Rahid Pavic [phoen], Ibrahim Salkic, Dedo Halilovic, Aziz Hecimovic, Osman Mesic, Pasaga Tihic, Esad Hadzimujagic, Fuad Jasenica and others. Nevertheless, most of the concrete work was done by Izet and Alija. That's Izetbegovic, right, who went to Slavonski Brod, to Metaric [phoen] and Piplovic, and this is in Croatia, I add. And once they brought 100 kilograms of explosive from there, and another time 10.000 bullets, 20 grenades, some anti-tank shells. Izet also, on one occasion, agreed upon and received from the party 30 automatic rifles and 5 pistols. During Ramazan, Senahid Memic once came before the mosque, a man from the party, because along the road to Samac his truck broke down. "Then I organised the goods to be loaded onto a different truck." Then there was the veterinary station -- that belonged the veterinary station: "Smajlovic transported the weapons to the destination, and for that service we got 20 automatic weapons and 2.000 bullets. In that way, we already had 50 automatic weapons. With these weapons, we equipped a platoon that patrolled town with hidden weapons primarily in vehicles. Depending on the situation, we had several patrols and then we covered all entrances into Bosanski Samac." Is that right, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me provide you with an answer. All the weapons that we had, all the weapons that we ensured, you just referred to them now, these were some automatic rifles, Klashnikovs. In relation to -- or, rather, in comparison to weapons of others, it was negligible. These weapons were in vehicles, it was not publicly displayed, and during the night we covered the entry points into Bosanski Samac. These guards of ours were trying to prevent bad things from happening at night, because different people would come to Bosanski Samac and different rumours were going around. And we did all of this in agreement with the police, the chief of police, who could not ensure a sufficient number of policemen in Bosanski Samac for protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vinko Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A Croat; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vinko Dragicevic is a Croat. He was the chief of the Public Security Station in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On one occasion, a patrol of the JNA entered Bosanski Samac and disarmed your patrol, and you erected barricades straight away. Alija Fitozovic organised this, and you say here in your statement that this happened without your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the JNA patrol came in and did what is written here, that is to say, when they seized the weapons from one of our patrols, Alija Fitozovic -- well, this caused the citizens to feel upset, and Alija Fitozovic organised barricades, although I was clearly against that, and I stated that clearly and said that that was not a good thing. I said that was not our method of struggle, that these barricades could only lead to problems. And there had already been barricades in Serb and Croat villages. I thought that this was not a good thing. And the very next day, we removed that, and the president of the SDS and the HDZ called upon all the citizens to do that and to remove all these barricades from Serb villages, Croat villages --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that, you fired at the patrol of the JNA that went to Bosanski Samac. Osman Mesic fired at it. He did not hit anyone. You say that he fired into the air, but in the direction of that patrol. And then that patrol went away, and you were afraid that the JNA would come back with stronger forces, and you removed the barricades immediately, and you were also afraid that the 4th Detachment would be activated. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.
