utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was against barricades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was against barricades. That is to say, I believe that this was not a smart thing to do, and I wanted to have these barricades removed the same morning. That was not a good thing, and that was demonstrated by the fact that Osman Mesic fired into the air in the direction from where the military police was coming in, and that could lead to a conflict. Also, there was the 4th Detachment there. There were armed Serbs who could fire at the backs of those who were in barricades. So this was a stupid and irresponsible move, and I did my best to have these barricades removed as soon as possible; not because the JNA would come -- well, perhaps on account of that, too, but primarily because I thought that this was not a good thing, generally speaking. It's not a good thing for a town, for any place, to have barricades there and to have check-points of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You believed that nothing could be achieved through barricades?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that was wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, when you removed the barricades, then you joined in a daily cooperation with the HDZ by way of preparations, and you say: "Cooperation was reflected in agreements reached between political representatives, daily contacts between our commander and their commander, and at the first meeting in Prud." They agreed with you that a joint Crisis Staff should be established; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I have to answer this, because this is very important. I came to this meeting after it had started, and I saw that only the representatives of the Bosniaks and the Croats were there and that the intention was to establish a staff for the municipality of Samac consisting only of Croats and Bosniaks. I then said that I was against that, that we could not have only two peoples establishing a staff, that the third people had to be made aware, too. Then the staff was not established. I personally was against that, and it was not established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here you insisted that the two staffs continued existing in parallel; that Alija Fitozovic remained the commander of your staff and on that occasion the Croats gave you one PAP semi-automatic rifle against anti-tank mines and grenades.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was against the establishment of a staff for Bosanski Samac municipality consisting only of Bosniaks and Croats. I wanted the Serbs to be included. I wanted it to be a real Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. After that meeting, you get another shipment of weapons from Croatia, that's what we read in your statement, around 50 automatic rifles, 2 mortars, several Zolja, hand-held rocket-launchers, right? That's what Zoljas are?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Croatia, as I said, 50 automatic rifles were brought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. These are a new 50, so in total you have 100 automatic rifles now?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to finish. Those 50 rifles, I said, should be brought to the Staff of the Territorial Defence, because it had been formed by that time. Until then, there had been no TO Staff. I was afraid that these automatic rifles would be distributed to civilians, that they would be used outside of any control, and I wanted them to be turned over to the TO Staff. And that was done. And then two days later, Samac was attacked and those weapons were found there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your statement says something different. It says: "Most of the weapons were immediately distributed in the TO Staff, mainly to Muslims, and several to Croats." Here it is on page 14 of your statement. So these weapons did not remain in the Staff. You immediately distributed them at the Staff.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe every word you said.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to let the interpreters finish. The fact is the weapons were turned over to the Territorial Defence Staff. Now, to what extent, within those two or three days before the attack on Samac, those weapons were successfully distributed, whether most of them were or not, I don't know. All I know is that when Samac was attacked, some of those weapons were found at the Territorial Defence Staff, which was a legal institution, and it was legally distributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can that TO Staff be a legal institution when it was outside any control by the JNA? Only a territorial defence under strict control of the JNA was legal, under the decision of the Presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the way it was, that's not the way it was. The TO Staff was appointed by the Republic Staff of Territorial Defence. It was completely legal. And the Command of the TO Staff was under the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they acted upon their orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in Samac, when you were captured, you called that war, and you say perhaps 15 to 20 days before the war, there was a clash between members of the 4th Detachment and members of the reserve police, and you state the names of those involved in the clash, and we see that there were Muslims on both sides, both in the 4th Detachment controlled the JNA, and the reserve police controlled by you, and you gave us the name of the Muslims in the reserve police; Mesad Mesic, Nizam Ramusovic -- no, no, reserve police, Adis Izetbegovic, Sead Srna, and one policeman from Hasici?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Croat, all right. And on the other side, Nizam Ramusovic, Mesad Mesic and Daniluk [phoen], that one could be a Serb, right, in the 4th Detachment. So on both sides in that first skirmish, there were Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, those were members of the 4th Detachment -- we should wait for the interpreters. Members of the 4th Detachment were provocative on that day. They were shooting at a tavern where there were members and followers of the SDA, and at the time as they were shooting, a police patrol came by. And not knowing who's shooting and what happened, and thinking that they were the target, they started fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's interesting, Mr. Tihic, is that only three members of the 4th Detachment were wounded, two Muslims and one Serb, and that none of your reserve policemen were wounded. And now you say they were the first to shoot. Maybe they really did shoot first, but in the air. But they got shot there. All three of them were wounded.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to wait for the interpretation. The police patrol heard and saw shooting. They didn't know whether they were the targets, whether they were going to be missed or shot, so they fired back. But the fact is the people from the 4th Detachment started shooting first. It is an unfortunate incident, but those from the 4th Detachment shot first, and the people who were coming in that direction could not know if that was shooting in the air, so they fired back. And so it happened that these people were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you, when you were captured, Mr. Tihic, had an automatic rifle and a pistol on you; right? You hid the pistol, and the automatic rifle was taken away from you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was captured, I was in the house of Mica Pavlovic, a neighbour of mine, without any weapons. But earlier on, I had been issued with a pistol and an automatic rifle that were back there at my house, and they were taken away when my house was searched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, by all appearances the JNA arrested you quite legally. You had weapons, you were an insurgent, and everything was legal except the frequent beatings that you were subjected to after your arrest. That part I condemn, too, and I believe the people responsible for beating you and the other prisoners should be held accountable. Why they are not held accountable is a question best addressed to the Prosecution, but the intervention of the JNA was legal and your arrest was legal because you were armed, you were members of armed units. Whether you had the weapons on you or not is not particularly important here.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a legal attack of the JNA against the town of Bosanski Samac. It was not legal for the JNA to come to occupy the police station, to occupy the municipal building, to drive out all the officials who were non-Serbs, all the policemen who were non-Serbs. And speaking of the JNA, it could have remained where it had been, in Serbian villages, but it was not supposed to change the government. It was not its job to change the government, all the more so because nobody was attacking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief, you described how JNA helicopters arrived and brought some members of special units, that is, soldiers you called specialised soldiers, and they were in fact soldiers who had gone through specialised training and were to be the core of the 4th Detachment; do you know that? Do you know that among these soldiers who were brought by helicopters of the JNA, there were also people from Bosanski Samac who had been previously sent to training and then came back together with soldiers from Serbia, including some volunteers?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you all I know about these helicopters. I told you that a Serb person came to my office, told me that two helicopters had arrived, brought these members of special units from Serbia who imposed the terror on those villages, beat up some guards even. Now, who was in those helicopters, whether that included people from Bosanski Samac who had gone to some special training, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I do know. You don't have to believe me. And then you go on to say: "I later learned that the Red Berets were part of the police force in Serbia." Now, only the fact that these soldiers were wearing red berets, although it was indubitable they were members of the JNA and had arrived by JNA helicopters, is enough for you to link them with the special unit of the MUP of Serbia established in 1996, whose members also had red berets; is that correct? What is the connection of the Serbian police force with these people who came by helicopter and wore red berets?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you. They came by helicopter. They were wearing military uniform. I was told that they were Red Berets. I thought they were part of the Serbian police force. Now you're telling me they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that some units of the JNA also wore red berets?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but they came as part of the JNA, as part of the army. Whether they were formally under the control of the JNA or the police, that's something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you mentioned Zvezdan Jovanovic, because you had information that he worked for the police later, and you know very well that it's possible that he had been in the JNA, then in Arkan's Volunteers Guard, and then moved on to the police force. When this special unit was established in 1996, many former Arkan's men joined that unit. They also looked for some volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, but since we were in fierce conflict with the regime, we refused. But Arkan's men joined that unit. And now you say Zvezdan Jovanovic was a notorious criminal, he killed and robbed, et cetera. But nobody could say, in Serbia, about Zvezdan Jovanovic, that he was a robber. Not even at the trial for the murder of Prime Minister Djindjic could anyone say that.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that he robbed and that he was a criminal on the basis of what he did in Bosanski Samac. One of my relatives filled in, on his orders, blank driving licenses that had previously been seized from Muslims. My relative was a civilian. He typed out illegal driving licenses for Zvezdan Jovanovic, put stamps on them so that Zvezdan Jovanovic could take out these cars to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April/May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the withdrawal of the JNA from Samac? That's absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the same way they seized rifles, weapons. They forged licenses to carry weapons. They took out all sorts of equipment from trucks. They looted machinery. The local Serbs did not dare to protest, because these were dangerous people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I am absolutely certain that there was no major looting. There may have been petty theft and pilfering, but nothing looted left Bosnia-Herzegovina before the JNA left. The looting began after the JNA left, but you were not in Samac then. You are telling us about hearsay. Whether that man was really Zvezdan Jovanovic or not, that's in great doubt. I have no reason to defend him, because I have never seen him in my life, but all of Serbia knows that he was not a criminal, that he was not a robber. He was a very professional soldier. Whether he killed Djindjic or not, I personally do not believe it. The trial took place in very suspicious circumstances. One day, the truth will come out. Certain things were fabricated, and before the trial, the police executed two key witnesses, this man Siptar and the other Lukovic. Those are facts, Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that these two units, these specials, were also robbers and looters. They looted the private property of citizens. They looted the socially-owned property of enterprises. And Zvezdan Jovanovic was one of them. I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From hearsay?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From talking to Bosniaks, from talking to Serbs. Later on, of course, when all this was in the past and when we talked, and even Serbs told me how they had tried to stand up to it, but they did not dare to because these were dangerous people, as I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is all hearsay. You know that, but never mind. Do you know that after the withdrawal of the JNA, this 4th Detachment that belonged to the 17th Tactical Group, grew into the Semberija Brigade of the army of Republika Srpska? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have an occasion to talk while the Judges are busy, because my time is running out.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want the Judges to hear what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They'll read it later.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you told me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One minute, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we were computing the time with the Registrar. You have almost used up all of your time. You have one last question, and then we will put an end to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have, I have asked my question, and now I'm waiting for the answer of Mr. Tihic, who didn't want to answer until he was sure you were listening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told me that all I know about looting is hearsay. I know about it firsthand. They robbed me, personally, these specials. They took me to my home and they made me turn over valuables to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who? You mentioned Lugar?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lugar was there, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the statement you gave to the investigators of the OTP, you said Lugar was a blonde, fair-haired man?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not dare look at these people in the face. As soon as they showed up, you had to look down, and you were not allowed to look at them carefully. When they showed me the picture, I recognised him, but I said, "I'm not quite sure." But I did identify him. He was stalkier then, and especially since he was wearing a uniform. But let me answer the question about the 4th Detachment which you say grew into a Brigade of the VRS. I did hear the same thing, that this 4th Detachment later grew into a Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Posavina Brigade. And as for this Lugar man, your statement says he was blonde. And I met him quite by chance once in my life, and I know that he had jet black hair. He hasn't been alive for a long time now and it doesn't matter, but he had black hair.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lugar was the worst criminal there. He beat me up very badly. I don't know about his hair. I was very frightened of him, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know what I meant to say. Human memory is not quite reliable, Mr. Tihic, especially after such a long time. I believe that somebody beat you up badly. You would not have made that story up, not at this length. I believe that you were beaten. But after a certain time, people are inclined, in their thinking, to ascribe their suffering to some people about whom they learn only later. Now, it's difficult to identify, name by name, all the people who beat you, but do you agree that you blame most the man who was the chief of the Security Service, and he is the one who should identify perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lugar beat me up several times, personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never mind. He's not the subject of our conversation. My final question, and this is my final question: Do you agree that for all the beatings that you suffered from the first time you were captured until you were exchanged, that the main culprit and the main person responsible was the chief of the Security Service?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a number of culprits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it's up to him to find who the perpetrators were and who the culprits were, but you and I both know who that is. Thank you, Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, I have a follow-up question I would like some details. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your municipality, the TO was set up. You explained this. This TO is made up of Muslims. There were weapons, 50 pistols and more rifles and so on. Fine. We see exactly what happened. We know that the captain in charge had set up some barricades. You were against that. Fine. But now I would like to put a question to the legal expert, to the lawyer. Obviously, all this was happening in April 1992. As far as you know, did the Republic of Bosnia -- as far as you know, could you tell us when the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina declared its independence?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina organised a referendum on the 29th of February and the 1st of March, 1992, that is, and the European Union recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 6th of April, 1992, and then later on it was recognised by all the other countries. And on the 20th of May, it became a member of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on the 19th of May, the JNA withdrew, and until the JNA withdrew, Mr. President, it could not have become a member of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You just mentioned dates, dates that are extremely important, of course. On April 6th, 1992, the European Union recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, if I understand correctly, the TO started operating after April 6th, 1992, after the European Union had recognised the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign and independent state; is that it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence existed before, within the framework of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, with the proviso that the JNA for a year beforehand had disarmed the Territorial Defence and taken the weapons away. Now, in that Territorial Defence, the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established later on, from the 6th of April onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj took the floor and said that the JNA withdrew on May 19th. I believe that you must agree with him on this date of May 19th. However, as a lawyer, don't you think that the JNA should have withdrawn as early as April 6th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it should have withdrawn already on the 1st of March, when the referendum on independence was held and when Bosnia-Herzegovina, to all intents and purposes, became independent in official terms. But the JNA did not even withdraw on the 19th of April, when it officially should have done so, but they stayed on for a long time after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are saying that it should have withdrawn in March already?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at it from a formal standpoint, the results of the referendum were proclaimed, the citizens declared themselves in favour of independence, so the JNA had nothing to look for there anymore. It was a foreign army from that moment on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm sure we will have occasion to return to this issue at a latter stage. Mr. Mussemeyer, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: There's no need to redirect. But as for the personal notes of the witness has been quoted extensively, I think it should be moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, from what I understood, the witness wrote a book. I believe you quoted the exhibit number on the 65 ter list. If I remember correctly, that should be 2004. Is that the right number, 2004? 2094?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I shall turn to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2094, Mr. Mussemeyer, that is the book which you wish to tender; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The title is "Personal Notes of the Witness Sulejman Tihic." I will see what it says on the first page. It starts with "Memoirs," but I cannot see more, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like Mr. Tihic's statement to be tendered into evidence, the one we have before us, which was taken on - I'm just checking the date --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You wish this to be tendered also into evidence. In other words, you want two documents to be tendered into evidence. Registrar, can we have -- Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, it is absolutely impermissible for the statement to be admitted into evidence that the witness gave to the OTP. He testified viva voce, and all those statements given previously to the OTP go directly into the waste paper basket, whereas this is a document that was compiled far before the testimony itself, and this is, for example, a document that could be taken in under 89 ter. This is a typical document that could be subjected to that Rule, and not the statement given to the OTP and is written by the OTP. This is written personally by the witness, Mr. President, and the statement he gave to the OTP was written by either the Prosecutor or the investigator, based on the proofing session or interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It cannot be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The reason why we took this statement was the order of the Trial Chamber of the 7th of January, 2008, where it was said that we could come back with a 92 ter statement from the witness which is consolidated. We consolidated this statement, and after each paragraph it is said where we quoted from. It has been translated into the witness's language, and the witness read, made corrections, and then signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, it is important for you to remember that initially the Prosecutor wanted to hear this witness as a 92 ter witness, and the Trial Chamber at the time had asked the Prosecutor to provide it with a consolidated statement. And it is you, you yourself, who intervened and who said that you wanted Mr. Tihic to come and testify viva voce, in light of the role he had played and the position of this gentleman. The Trial Chamber had said that we would deliberate on the matter, which we did, and the Trial Chamber agreed to what you had asked for and decided that this witness would come and testify as a viva voce witness. So this is how things stand. We understand now that you are telling us that what counts, when a viva voce comes to testify, is the transcript and not the statement. I shall turn to my colleagues to see what needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to tell you this: Any possible admittance of this statement into evidence would be a trick, because I was told that the witness would be testifying viva voce. I was preparing for that. He's testifying viva voce, and I cross-examined him. And now if, by some unfortunate circumstance, you were to admit his former statement under 92 ter, then that would be a unique example of a witness who testified viva voce and under 92 ter, and then I would consider myself to have been duped and tricked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall turn to my colleagues now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber, after having deliberated, as you could see, decides: (A), that the personal notes entitled "Memoirs" or so-called memoirs, are admitted. The Registrar will give us a number for this. However, as far as the 92 ter statement is concerned, the Trial Chamber does not grant the Prosecutor's request. Could we have an exhibit number, therefore, Registrar, for Mr. Tihic's notes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given Exhibit number P681. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Mr. Tihic, your testimony has come to an end. Personally and on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to thank you for having come to testify, for having taken the time to come and testify in this case, and I would like to thank you for the answers you provided to the questions put to you by the Prosecution, by Mr. Seselj and by the Bench. We wish you a safe journey home, and we wish you all the best in your future endeavours. I shall ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom, but my colleague has something to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to add to what the Presiding Judge has just said, the expression of our deep compassion for the pain and the suffering that you have endured. It seems that you have suffered more than most, and the Chamber recognises the courage and the efforts you have taken to come here and testify again about this. And we wish you, as we wish all witnesses who have been exposed to suffering during the war, our best hopes for the life in the future for all of you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move into closed session, I have something to say. Mr. Mundis will then have the floor. Mr. Seselj, yesterday I stepped in at one stage because when you spoke, you talked about demanding something, and I had said that this might be a question of semantics, due to the translation of what you had said. You then stepped in and said that in your country, this could arise, you could step in and intervene during the proceedings and say that you demanded something. After having looked into the matter, it seems that you were partly right. Lawyers in Serbia use this particular term. I wanted this to be on the record. I wasn't challenging anything when I said this yesterday, but in civil law countries I believe things are very similar to the way they happen in your country. The accused make requests, and one responds to these requests. In exceptional circumstances, demands are made when an accused, for instance, wishes to have a lawyer. That is a demand, per se, and the Bench needs to respond to that. This is what I had to say to you to make sure there is no ambiguity whatsoever. I am concerned about the fact that these proceedings should unfold in the best possible conditions, as smoothly as possible, and that the witnesses are able to respond as they should. This is our objective, an objective we share with all the people concerned. This is what I had to say about this matter. I would like to move into closed session now, because I would like to know what our schedule is. Mr. Mundis, was that why you were on your feet?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something to say briefly in open session, before you move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yesterday I received a request from the Prosecution that a written statement of VS-1033, under 92 ter, be admitted, and it was on the 19th of November, that is, the date of the request, and it was handed to me yesterday. And I categorically oppose it, because I consider there is no reason why this witness should be heard under 92 ter and that he should come in here and be heard viva voce. Now, referring to all the arguments that I have put forth umpteen times as to why I do not accept anything under 92 ter, I don't want to repeat myself and take up more time, but those arguments stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As has occurred previously, we shall look into the matter. Sometimes we stand by what we say. Sometimes we agree to what you are saying. We shall let you know very quickly, and we shall hand down a decision on this matter. Mr. Mundis, let's move into closed session or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did I hear this right? In the morning next week, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, we're sitting in the morning, Tuesday morning at 8.30. We'll tell you as soon as possible, maybe this afternoon, as early as this afternoon, about the time allocation. But I believe from what the Prosecutor said, that these will be witnesses that will not take up a lot of time. Yes, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just remembered, Mr. President, what it was that I thought was important. May I say it now? In advance, I'm absolutely opposed to having the Prosecution time extended for their case, because I have proof that the Prosecution has not used their time so far rationally. For example, these last two witnesses, from the point of view of the indictment and from the point of view of what it is that they are trying to prove, these last two witnesses were brought here for no reason whatsoever. You see that both have nothing to do with the indictment issued against me. Mr. Tihic did not contribute at all to providing evidence of a pattern of behaviour in Bosanski Samac. He just told us the story of his fate or destiny, and that's it. As for Mr. Fadil Banjanovic, he also spoke about the crime base, and it is two months removed from the period when volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were in the territory of Zvornik, and he never saw them in Kozluk. So two witnesses that were brought here totally unnecessarily. They were useful for me, but not for the Prosecution. This is a strong argument, from my point of view, that no additional time should be given to the Prosecution for presenting their case. I could give you a series of examples in relation to previous witnesses that were also used, and there was no point in doing that, from the point of view of the indictment, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I understood, the Prosecutor told us it was just a working assumption, he's thinking about it, but if he is asking for additional time, he will submit a motion. This motion must be grounded with motivations and so on, and I'm sure you will be allowed to reply also. But right now, this is just a working assumption, that they might need an extension. Nothing has been set as of now, and the Trial Chamber hasn't been seized of any motion as of now. This is where we stand. So I would like to thank you all, and we will resume on Tuesday morning, 8.30 a.m. thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of December, 2008, at 8.30 a.m. 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.40 a.m.,
